PROJECTS

**OVC Project (Orphans and Vulnerable Children)**

We strengthen the wellbeing of orphans and vulnerable children through case management, health referrals, psychosocial support, child protection, and caregiver empowerment to ensure every child grows in a safe, supportive environment.

**Bee Keeping Project**

We promote climate-smart livelihoods by supporting farmers with modern beehives, training, and market linkage—improving incomes while enhancing pollination and environmental conservation.

**SACCO Project**

We build household economic resilience through savings and credit groups, financial literacy, and support to small enterprises, enabling families to access affordable credit and grow their incomes.

**Bicycles Project**

We improve access to education and health services by providing bicycles to learners and community volunteers, reducing distance barriers and saving time for essential services.

**Digital Literacy Skills Project**

We equip children, youth, and caregivers with essential digital skills for learning, communication, and opportunity in an increasingly digital world.

**HES Project (Household Economic Strengthening)**

We empower caregivers with skills in budgeting, savings, nutrition, provide business boost, productive assets and small enterprise development to improve household stability and child wellbeing.

**Computer Class Project**

We provide structured computer lessons that build practical skills in typing, basic applications, and introductory coding to prepare learners for academic and career success.

ECONOMIC EMPOWERMENT

**BOSINESS BOOST**

**From Struggle to Success: How a Business Grant Transformed X’s Cereal Business**

X, a caregiver of one Female OVC in the program who scored CPARA score of 7 with gaps in Stable domain and School domain, had always dreamt of running her own business. Living in a modest neighborhood (Adungosi Town) she began with a small table outside her home where she sold cereals like cowpeas, black night shade, Amaranthus, Sorghum beans, and millet to locals. Despite her dedication, limited capital meant she could only stock small quantities, and often had to turn customers away.

Juggling motherhood and business was no easy feat. Her income barely covered household expenses and school fees. But X was determined to build something better for herself and her family.

On 17th December 2025 a few months later, she received the life-changing news: She received Ksh.8000 from USAID4TheChild through ADT after being assessed and trained on small business management skills.

With the Business grant/boost, X was able to:

* Increase her stock of cereals significantly, buying in bulk to reduce costs.  
* Rent a small market cabinet/stall in Adungosi Market instead of selling outside in the open.  
* Introduce grocery items such as tomatoes, onions, vegetables, and fruits (avocado) which attracted more foot traffic.

The expansion quickly paid off. Customers appreciated the convenience of buying both cereals and fresh produce in one place. Her daily income more than tripled, and she was able to reinvest her profits to maintain a steady and diverse stock.

Today, X’s shop is a staple in her community. Most importantly, she can now comfortably support her child’s education even after completing her secondary school education and has a renewed sense of confidence and purpose.

“The boost didn’t just grow my business — it gave me hope. It reminded me that as a mother, I’m not limited. I’m empowered. I’m able to save Ksh.350a week in our Saving Group’’

X’s story is a testament to what passion, resilience, and the right support can do for a woman with a dream.

**2nd Business Monitored**  
X is a dedicated caregiver of three children though one only is enrolled in the program, is among the beneficiaries of the USAID 4TheChild project aimed at strengthening the economic resilience of vulnerable households caring for CALHIV, orphans and vulnerable children (OVC). Before receiving support, she was running a small cereal business with very limited capital, barely able to meet her family's basic needs.  
In October 2024, she was identified as a suitable candidate for economic empowerment and was awarded a business grant (KES 8,000). The grant was intended to boost her existing cereal-selling business.  
With the capital injection, she restocked a wider variety of cereals in bulk, including Amaranthus, cow peace, soya beans, maize, beans, and green grams, which allowed her to attract more customers and increase her daily sales. Due to high demand of cereal items, the stock is always consumed at a high rate as shown in Fig 8  
The profits earned have enabled her to:

* Expand her tailoring business, which she had temporarily abandoned due to lack of capital.  
* Pay school fees for her son who is in Form 2 at Butula Boys high school.  
* Settle rent and utility bills on time, reducing household stress and instability.  
* Afford medical expenses.


  
She now runs both the cereal and tailoring businesses concurrently. Her vision is to open a small tailoring workshop and train young girls in her community while continuing to supply cereals to nearby schools and markets.  
This success story highlights the transformative power of economic empowerment for caregivers. The support from USAID 4TheChild has not only strengthened her household's financial stability but also restored her dignity and hope.

**ECONOMIC EMPOWERMENT**  
**Productive assets beneficiaries.**  
**1st Beneficiary**  
Productive assets, like equipment and technology, significantly impact small businesses by boosting productivity, streamlining operations, and enhancing profitability. These assets allow businesses to produce more goods or services efficiently, ultimately leading to increased revenue and market competitiveness. Asset tracking and management can also improve efficiency, reduce operational costs, and help businesses make more informed decisions.  During this reporting period, 5 beneficiaries were monitored all-female supporting 18OVC (3m,15f). The beneficiaries received the productive assets in 2024 and they are really doing well in their business and for the case of Electine Ajiambo who comes from Angorom, Teso South Sub County with 2 OVC in the program (1m,1f) had a reason to smile after USAID 4TheChild program through ADT gave her a complete set of sewing machines. “A miracle happened”, she says. “I’m now self-employed has made me independent. I can stand on my own. I now earn enough money for my personal expenses.”

The caregiver feels proud to be able to help not only her family with everyday expenses but also her community with inexpensive clothes made in her tailoring shop.“I can contribute money for food purchases and I help with the purchase of school material for my children, which has meant a lot for my family”, she says. The caregiver saves sh.300 weekly in her Upendo Saving group. 

**2nd Beneficiary**

This is Nabwire, a caregiver in Marachi Central who received the Umbrella on 6th of Nov 2024 as seen in the picture. The caregiver has 4OVC in the program (2m,2f) Nabwire sales her cereals in an open-air market. Before receiving the umbrella, Nabwire business was not that much thriving. She used to report to the market center in the evening when the sun is setting. ‘Thank you to USAID 4TheChild for the precious gift, I can now report to my business site as early as 10am and sale my cereals the all day regardless how sunny that will be,” She said

**3rd Beneficiary**

 The caregiver X a mother of 1 female ovc who comes from Malaba Central ward, Teso North Sub County, Busia County with unique skills of dress repair and making. Before USAID4TheChild intervened, the caregiver was struggling with harsh living condition. She had good skills in cloth repair and making but lacked a productive asset (full set of sewing machine) to earn a living through her skills. 

 ‘Thank you USAID4TheChild through ADT for coming to my rescue’ She said after receiving a full set of sewing machine and later on joined ‘HOUSE OF COZACK’ company that purely does tailoring job.  The company was established in 2018 and secures good paying tenders thus providing good payment to its employee. The caregiver is currently able to pay rent, cover medical cost, provide food and school fees for her children and currently she was paid Ksh.10,000 that she used to buy building materials for her house.

**4th Beneficiary**

The caregiver X who prepares samosa in Lukolis Market. The caregiver received a Displaying box, cooking pan and cooking spoon. Before USAID4TheChild came into her rescue, her business was not thriving. She used to sale her samosa in a plastic green bucket thus not attracting customers. Her stock could even last for 2 days before it is consumed by the customers. Currently, the caregiver is happier for the assets she received from the project through ADT. The displaying box has enhanced brand visibility, increased sales, and improves customer satisfaction. A visually appealing presentation has attracted more customers and encouraged impulse purchases, while also reinforcing a brand's image and offering a sense of quality. Additionally, the box is protecting the samosas from moisture and contamination, ensuring they remain fresh and flavorful. 

**Enhanced Brand Visibility and Image: **

* Professional Presentation: The display box is more attractive thus, elevate the perceived value and quality of the samosas, building a more professional brand image.

* Aesthetic Appeal: Eye-catching designs and color have made samosas stand out on shelves and attract customers

**Increased Sales and Customer Satisfaction:**

* Impulse Purchases: The box is visually appealing thus, encouraging customers to buy on impulse, especially if they are already browsing. 

* Quality Perception: The box suggests a higher quality product, leading to increased customer satisfaction and repeat purchases. 

* Freshness and Taste: The box has been designed to protect samosas from moisture and contamination, ensuring they stay fresh and flavorful. 

**Streamlined Operations:**

* Easy Transportation: Display box has made it easy to transport samosas without damage or mess. 

* Organization: The box has helped keep samosas organized and easy to access for both the seller and the customer. 

In conclusion, displaying samosas in attractive and functional box is a crucial aspect of a samosa seller's business, contributing to increased sales, brand visibility, and customer satisfaction. Thanks to USAID4TheChild project. The caregiver is making a profit of Ksh.350 after every sale. Now she is able to provide school fees to her children, buy food, buy farm input, clear medical expenses and other basic needs in the household.

**ENVIRONMENTAL MITIGATION STORY**

**Caregivers linked to Nutrition in City Ecosystem (NICE) program.**

The Nutrition in City Ecosystems (NICE) Project is supported by the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC). It focuses on six initial secondary cities in Bangladesh, Kenya, and Rwanda to improve health and nutrition and contribute to reducing poverty for populations of city regions, especially women, youth and vulnerable groups.

The NICE Project facilitates locally-led action for improved nutrition in low- and middle-income countries through agricultural, food and health sector collaborations, and public-private engagements, with strong emphasis on the role of women and youth entrepreneurs.

The NICE Project facilitates locally-led action for improved nutrition in low- and middle-income countries through agricultural, food and health sector collaborations, and public-private engagements, with strong emphasis on the role of women and youth entrepreneurs.

![][image4]

***Figure 26 shows a man-made fish pond made out of timber and black nylon paper courtesy of NICE knowledge*** 

The project works to strengthen linking between demand for and production and availability of nutritious foods produced using agroecological practices. Further, the city-knowledge hubs ensure horizontal and vertical exchange, thereby shaping urban-rural food environments and informing national and global policies. During this reporting period, 6caregivers all female were linked to NICE where they were trained on good practice of organic farming to improve productivity.

 Agricultural knowledge is crucial for effective use of farm inputs, leading to increased efficiency, productivity, and profitability. Caregivers were trained on how to properly use and manage inputs like organic fertilizers, pesticides, seeds, and machinery as one of the essentials for maximizing crop yields and minimizing environmental impact. This knowledge also enables farmers to make informed decisions about input choices, timing of application, and overall farm management practices. 

1\. Optimized Input Use:

* **Knowledge about soil health and nutrient requirements:**

Farmers need to understand their soil's characteristics (pH, nutrient content) to select the appropriate fertilizers and use them efficiently, preventing over-fertilization and environmental damage. 

* **Understanding pest and disease management:**

Knowing the specific pest and disease problems on their crops allows farmers to choose the right control measures and use them effectively, minimizing pesticide use and potential harm to beneficial insects and the environment. 

* **Proper seed selection and planting techniques:**

Choosing the right seed varieties for their region, soil type, and climate, and using appropriate planting methods, are critical for maximizing yield and success. 

* **Efficient use of machinery:**

Understanding how to operate and maintain farm equipment, including tractors, combines, and other machinery, is essential for optimizing work efficiency and minimizing breakdowns. 

2\. Increased Productivity and Profitability:

* **Higher yields:**

Using the right inputs in the right amounts and at the right time, as dictated by agricultural knowledge, can significantly increase crop yields. 

* **Reduced input costs:**

By optimizing input use and avoiding waste, farmers can reduce their costs and improve their profit margins. 

* **Improved crop quality:**

Proper input management can lead to crops that are healthier, more nutritious, and of higher quality, which can command higher prices in the market. 

3\. Sustainable and Responsible Farming Practices:

* **Promoting sustainable agricultural practices:**

By understanding best practices for soil health, water management, and pest control, farmers can adopt sustainable farming methods that ensure long-term productivity and environmental integrity. 

4\. Access to Information and Technology:

* **Agricultural extension services:**

Many countries have agricultural extension services that provide farmers with training and information on various aspects of agriculture, including input management. 

* **Online resources and mobile apps:**

Farmers can access a wealth of information and resources online, including mobile apps that provide information on input recommendations, weather forecasts, and market prices. 

In conclusion, agricultural knowledge is fundamental to the success of modern farming. It enables farmers to make informed decisions about input use, optimize productivity, promote sustainable practices, and contribute to a more resilient and efficient food system. 

**LIVELIHOOD AND ECONOMIC EMPOWERMENT**

**From Shamba Boy to Skilled Youth: A Transformational Journey of a CALHIV Youth**

Meet *X* (not his real name) an 18-year-old adolescent living with HIV (CALHIV), whose inspiring journey reflects resilience, transformation, and hope.

X dropped out of school in Class 4 due to poverty, stigma, and health-related challenges. With no stable support system at home, he left for Eldoret in search of survival and ended up working as a *shamba boy* (farm help). Life was tough — long hours, minimal pay, and little hope for the future. 

His life took a turning point when he was rescued through the USAID 4TheChild Project. Growing up with limited resources and facing the challenges associated with living with HIV, X had few opportunities to build a stable future. The project, which supports vulnerable children and adolescents in Teso South Sub County, Chakol North Ward, Apegei village where he comes from, offered X a lifeline through mentorship, psychosocial support, and an opportunity to reclaim his future that helped him gain both technical skills and self-confidence.

X was recruited into an apprenticeship program and enrolled in *Komesha Tyre and Repair Services Company* in Busia Town in June 2024 to pursue a course. USAID 4TheChild paid all the fees required to complete the course as shown in figure 4\.  Through determination and support, he successfully completed the training in December 2024, gaining practical skills and self-confidence. 

Today, X is employed at DC Energy Petrol Station in Mundika Busia-Kisumu Road, where he earns a daily income of at least KES 500, enabling him to live independently and support himself. He is able to pay his house rent of KES 3,000 per month. 

 X dreams of one day opening his own tyre repair workshop and mentoring other young people facing similar challenges. However, he is humbly requesting the program to buy for him Tyre opening machine costing KES 10,000 and other important tools costing KES 5,000.

X's story is a testament to how targeted support and empowerment can help vulnerable adolescents transition into productive adulthood. He now proudly contributes to his household, manages his health responsibly, and aspires to one day own his own tyre repair shop.

This success highlights the transformative impact of the USAID 4TheChild Project in promoting resilience, self-reliance, and economic empowerment among young people living with HIV. The USAID 4TheChild Project continues to empower adolescents like X — restoring dignity, building livelihoods, and shaping bright futures.

**DIGITAL LITERACY SKILL**

**Agnes Wakoli- Unlocking new opportunity in Business with new Digital skills**

In Aterait village, Chakol North ward, Teso south sub county, a cereal business woman, Agnes Wakoli who was trained by CDC Paul Odokoh, struggling to compete with larger businesses, learned digital marketing and e-commerce, transforming her business from a small shop to a thriving online presence, showcasing her unique skills to a wider audience and significantly boosting her income. 

Here's a more detailed look at Agnes’ story:

* **Initial Challenges:**

Agnes faced challenges in reaching a wider audience and competing with larger, established businesses that could afford traditional advertising and marketing. Her cereal shop, while known locally, struggled to grow beyond its immediate community. 

* **The Turning Point: Digital Skills Training:**

Recognizing the need to adapt to the changing market, Agnes participated in a KICTANET digital skills training program, learning about social media marketing, e-commerce platforms, and online advertising. 

* **Online Transformation:**

Armed with these new skills, Agnes created a vibrant online presence, showcasing her unique cereal shop on platforms like Facebook. She learned to use engaging visuals, write compelling product descriptions, and leverage targeted advertising to reach potential customers beyond Aterait. 

* **E-commerce Success:**

Agnes set up Facebook store, allowing customers to purchase her cereals directly from her. She also explored options for selling on online marketplaces, expanding her reach even further. 

* **Positive Impact:**

Agnes’ digital transformation led to a remarkable increase in sales and a significant boost in her income. She was able to acquire more products, expand her shop. 

* **Community Impact:**

Agnes’ success story serves as an inspiration to other entrepreneurs in Aterait, demonstrating the power of digital skills to drive economic growth and create opportunities. 

* **Wide Reach:**

Agnes’ cereal shop once only available locally, are now enjoyed by customers around the wide range, thanks to her newfound digital skills. 

* **Continued Learning:**

Agnes remains committed to continuous learning, staying updated on the latest digital trends and technologies to maintain her competitive edge.

**SUCCESS STORY 2**

**Assistant Chief – A Dream come through.**

Asale Joseph, a 60-year administrator (Assistant Chief Amongura Sub Location) initially found using a smart phone confusing and frustrating. With the support of the CDC, he gradually learned the basics and was thrilled when he successfully sent his first email.

Joseph’s journey didn’t stop there. He explored applications like google meet, realizing that digital skills opened doors to social connection and personal growth. He is now equipped to navigate social media responsibly, use online meetings and social connectivity, and protect his privacy and security. Joseph is grateful to KICTANET for providing him with these valuable skills.

**SCHOOL FEES SUPPORT**

**RISING ABOVE – AMANI’S JOURNEY OF HOPE AND RESILIENCE THROUGH OVC SUPPORT**

In December 2019, the household in Awata village, Malaba North Ward, Teso North Sub-County, Busia County, was enrolled into the OVC project under the eligibility criteria of Persons Living with HIV. Among the household’s six school-going children (four girls and two boys) was Amani, a bright and determined girl with a deep passion for education.

Amani, now 13 years old, is currently a Form 2 student at Cheptiret Secondary School. She excelled in her 2023 KCPE examinations while at Kakokli Primary School, scoring an impressive 376 marks a testament to her academic strength and determination despite the many challenges at home. However, her journey through secondary school has not been smooth.

Coming from a family with limited financial resources, staying consistently in school became a challenge due to high school fees. Shortly after her admission into Form 1 in early 2024, she faced the risk of dropping out. Recognizing the urgency of her situation, the case worker alerted her case manager, who immediately escalated the issue to the OSDC. Following guidance, the caregiver applied for school fees support, and by July 23, 2024, the project intervened and cleared Ksh 15,000 in school fees arrears. Amani was retained in school an act that greatly eased her mental stress and renewed her academic focus.

During the May 2024 school holiday, Amani attended a beneficiary engagement meeting at Amagoro DIDC Hall. There, she confidently spoke to her peers, sharing how she consistently ranked among the top students despite her family’s hardships. She thanked the Amagoro satellite office and staff especially her case worker, Ursula Odera for their unwavering support, noting how such gatherings inspired and uplifted her.

In August 2024, the household underwent a CPARA assessment and scored 7 out of 9 benchmarks, missing only benchmark 5 and 9\. The project team took proactive steps by linking the caregiver to the Achuas SILC group for economic empowerment. Additionally, gaps were identified in the schooling domain across all children. In October 2024, another OVC from the household (CPIMS ID 3553850\) was also supported with school fees, showing the program's holistic approach.

Despite these interventions, Amani’s struggles were not over. In January 2025, she was sent back home from school as her parent had not paid any school fees for the new term. She remained home until the caregiver managed to raise a small portion of the fees. The office once again stepped in, and Amani was awarded a further Ksh 20,000 in school fees support on April 30, 2025\. This timely intervention ensured she remained in school and was able to continue with her education uninterrupted.

Now in Form 2 and performing well, Amani beams with hope.As every time the school shared with the parent her performance, he forwarded the text to the case worker who also forwards to the case manager as in this year her performance were as follows:

You have shown me love and given me a sense of belonging since day one of this journey. May God bless you ADT USAID 4The Child and expand your limits as you continue helping others who suffer in silence. Thank you for ensuring I stay in school and continue chasing my dreams.
